\chapter{Farewells}
\label{ch:farewells}
\hlchaptermodality{4}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can end a Telugu conversation politely and choose a farewell that fits the situation.}

Telugu, like every Dravidian language, does not say a plain “goodbye.” It promises to return: \te{వెళ్ళి} \te{వస్తాను} — “having gone, I come back.”
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ḍa]{\te{డ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S123-letter-dda}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{౫} — what amount does it stand for? And one from further back: \te{ఉ}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{డ}}
\textbf{\te{డ}} — \emph{ḍa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ḍ}, it is \textbf{ḍa}.

You met it on an earlier page, in the middle of a word you already say:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{మీరు} \te{ఎలా} \te{ఉన్నారు}?} — how are you? (respectful)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{డ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{డ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{డ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{మీరు} \te{ఎలా} \te{ఉన్నారు}?  ·  \te{నమస్కారం}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{డ} three times, saying \emph{ḍa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{డ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{డ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ḍa}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[veḷḷu]{\te{వెళ్ళు} (veḷḷu) — \textquotedblleft{}go,\textquotedblright{} and \te{వచ్చు} (come)}

\label{lesson:TE-C04-vellu}



\begin{quote}
Two everyday verbs — and together they make the Telugu goodbye.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\te{వె}} (\emph{ve}) + \textbf{\te{ళ్ళు}} (\emph{ḷḷu}, a doubled retroflex \textbf{\te{ళ}} \emph{ḷ}) $\to$ \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళు}} (\emph{veḷḷu}). Its partner: \textbf{\te{వచ్చు}} (\emph{vaccu}, \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}) with the doubled \textbf{\te{చ్చ}} (\emph{cc}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{వెళ్ళు}} (\emph{veḷḷu}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\te{వచ్చు}} (\emph{vaccu}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}) are native Dravidian verbs. As commands they are whole words: \emph{veḷḷu!} (\textquotedblleft{}go!\textquotedblright{}), \emph{rā!} (\textquotedblleft{}come!\textquotedblright{}). You need both, because Telugu — like every Dravidian language — does not say a plain \textquotedblleft{}goodbye.\textquotedblright{} It says \textquotedblleft{}I go, and I \textbf{come back}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\te{వె} (\emph{ve}) + \te{ళ్ళు} (\emph{ḷḷu}, doubled retroflex \te{ళ} \emph{ḷ}) $\to$ \te{వెళ్ళు}. Its partner \te{వచ్చు} (\emph{vaccu}, “come”).
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}veḷḷu\textquotedblright{} (go) and \textquotedblleft{}vaccu\textquotedblright{} (come)
  \item why you need both to say goodbye (Telugu's farewell is \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do \emph{veḷḷu} and \emph{vaccu} mean, and why will you need them both to part? (\textquotedblleft{}Go\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}; the Telugu goodbye is \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[6]{\te{౬} — the Telugu numeral for 6}

\label{lesson:TE-S145-digit-6}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{డ} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{౪}?

One numeral this time, and it is read the way every numeral is read: as an amount.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{౬}}
\textbf{\te{౬}} is \textbf{six}.

Six is where the second half begins, and where a warning belongs: \textbf{\te{౬} is not the 6 you write, and it is not an E}. It is its own character, and the only way it becomes readable is by meeting it often enough that the resemblance stops mattering.

Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\section[veḷḷi vastānu]{\te{వెళ్ళి} \te{వస్తాను} (veḷḷi vastānu) — \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C04-velli-vastaanu}



\begin{quote}
The everyday Telugu goodbye — a promise, not a parting.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\te{వెళ్ళి}} (\emph{veḷḷi}, \textquotedblleft{}having gone\textquotedblright{}) is \emph{veḷḷu} + the \textquotedblleft{}-i\textquotedblright{} that means \textquotedblleft{}having …d.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\te{వస్తాను}} (\emph{vastānu}, \textquotedblleft{}I come/will come\textquotedblright{}) is from \emph{vaccu} (\textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}) + \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{వెళ్ళి} \te{వస్తాను}} = \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళి}} (\emph{veḷḷi}, \textquotedblleft{}having gone\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\te{వస్తాను}} (\emph{vastānu}, \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having gone, I come {[}back{]}},\textquotedblright{} i.e. \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back.\textquotedblright{} A Telugu speaker never signs off with a bare \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving\textquotedblright{} — that sounds final. Instead they promise return. It is the same \textquotedblleft{}go-and-come-back\textquotedblright{} farewell you meet across the Dravidian south (Tamil \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ}, Kannada \emph{hōgi baruttēne}, Malayalam \emph{pōyi varāṁ}) and echoing into the Indo-Aryan tracks (Bengali \emph{āshi}). The warm reply is \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళి} \te{రండి}} (\emph{veḷḷi raṇḍi}, \textquotedblleft{}go and come {[}back{]}\textquotedblright{}).

\textbf{Across the family — the same idea, five ways:}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}go and come back\textquotedblright{} (goodbye)} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Telugu} & \emph{veḷḷi vastānu} \\
Tamil & \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ} \\
Kannada & \emph{hōgi baruttēne} \\
Malayalam & \emph{pōyi varāṁ} \\
Bengali (Indo-Aryan) & \emph{āshi} (\textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The whole south — and, in Bengali, well beyond it — prefers a promise of return to a blunt farewell. The languages are not all related; the habit travelled anyway.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the \textquotedblleft{}having …d\textquotedblright{} participle}]
\emph{Veḷḷi} is Telugu's way of chaining actions: \textquotedblleft{}having gone, (then) I come.\textquotedblright{} Like its sisters, Telugu strings verbs with one in the participle form and the last one fully conjugated.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the goodbye — \emph{veḷḷi vastānu}
  \item its literal meaning (\textquotedblleft{}having gone, I come\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}I'll come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item the warm reply — \emph{veḷḷi raṇḍi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Telugu goodbye literally promise, and how do you answer? (\textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{}; reply \emph{veḷḷi raṇḍi}, \textquotedblleft{}go and come back\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rēpu kaluddām]{\te{రేపు} \te{కలుద్దాం} (rēpu kaluddām) — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C04-reepu-kaluddaam}



\begin{quote}
A goodbye with a date on it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\te{రే}} (\emph{rē}) + \textbf{\te{పు}} (\emph{pu}) $\to$ \textbf{\te{రేపు}} (\emph{rēpu}). \textbf{\te{కలుద్దాం}} (\emph{kaluddām}) = \emph{kalu} (\textquotedblleft{}meet\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{-ddām} (\textquotedblleft{}let's\textquotedblright{}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{రేపు}} (\emph{rēpu}, \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian. \textbf{\te{కలుద్దాం}} (\emph{kaluddām}, \textquotedblleft{}let's meet\textquotedblright{}) is from \textbf{\te{కలు}} (\emph{kalu}, \textquotedblleft{}to meet, to join\textquotedblright{}) — so the phrase is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tomorrow, let's meet},\textquotedblright{} the Telugu \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow.\textquotedblright{} The \textbf{-\te{దాం}} (\emph{-ddām}) ending is Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}let's \_\_\_\textquotedblright{} — a first-person-plural invitation: \emph{veḷḷddām} (\textquotedblleft{}let's go\textquotedblright{}), \emph{tindām} (\textquotedblleft{}let's eat\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\te{రే} (\emph{rē}) + \te{పు} (\emph{pu}) $\to$ \te{రేపు}. \te{కలుద్దాం} (\emph{kaludḍām}) = \emph{kalu} (“meet”) + \emph{-dḍām} (“let's”).
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rēpu kaluddām\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{} (\emph{rēpu}, \emph{kalu})
  \item the \textquotedblleft{}let's \_\_\_\textquotedblright{} ending (\emph{-ddām})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \emph{rēpu kaluddām}, and what does \emph{-ddām} mean? (\emph{Rēpu} \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} + \emph{kalu} \textquotedblleft{}meet\textquotedblright{}; \emph{-ddām} = \textquotedblleft{}let's \_\_\_.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pa]{\te{ప} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S113-letter-pa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{౬} — what amount does it stand for? And one from further back: \te{ర}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{ప}}
\textbf{\te{ప}} — \emph{pa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{p}, it is \textbf{pa}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{ప} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \textbf{\te{రేపు} \te{కలుద్దాం}} \emph{rēpu kaluddām} — see you tomorrow
\end{itemize}

Put your pen on \te{ప} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\section[maḷḷī kaluddām]{\te{మళ్ళీ} \te{కలుద్దాం} (maḷḷī kaluddām) — \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C04-malli-kaluddaam}



\begin{quote}
The open-ended, warm goodbye — no date, just a promise.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\te{మళ్ళీ}} (\emph{maḷḷī}): note the doubled retroflex \textbf{\te{ళ్ళ}} (\emph{ḷḷ}), the same sound as in \emph{veḷḷu}. \textbf{\te{కలుద్దాం}} (\emph{kaluddām}, \textquotedblleft{}let's meet\textquotedblright{}) you just learned.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{మళ్ళీ} \te{కలుద్దాం}} = \textbf{\te{మళ్ళీ}} (\emph{maḷḷī}, \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\te{కలుద్దాం}} (\emph{kaluddām}, \textquotedblleft{}let's meet\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{we'll meet again}.\textquotedblright{} Both words are native Dravidian: \emph{maḷḷī} (\textquotedblleft{}again,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{maral}, \textquotedblleft{}to return\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{kalu} (\textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{}). Where Tamil's \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{} (\emph{mīṇḍum sandippōm}) reaches for the Sanskrit loan \emph{sandi} to say \textquotedblleft{}meet,\textquotedblright{} Telugu keeps the native \emph{kalu} — a small reminder that these sisters make the same phrase from different stock.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}maḷḷī kaluddām\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}let's meet\textquotedblright{} (\emph{maḷḷī}, \emph{kaluddām})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the phrase mean, and which Dravidian verb does Telugu use for \textquotedblleft{}meet\textquotedblright{} here? (\textquotedblleft{}We'll meet again\textquotedblright{}; the native \emph{kalu} — where Tamil used the Sanskrit loan \emph{sandi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[Practice]{Chapter 4 — The farewells}

\label{lesson:TE-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three ways to part — none of them a blunt \textquotedblleft{}goodbye.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — the farewells}
All three, side by side — none of them a blunt \textquotedblleft{}goodbye\textquotedblright{}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Telugu} & \textbf{} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\te{వెళ్ళి} \te{వస్తాను}.} & \emph{veḷḷi vastānu} & I'll go and come back. (the goodbye) \\
\textbf{\te{వెళ్ళి} \te{రండి}.} & \emph{veḷḷi raṇḍi} & Go and come back. (the reply) \\
\textbf{\te{రేపు} \te{కలుద్దాం}.} & \emph{rēpu kaluddām} & See you tomorrow. \\
\textbf{\te{మళ్ళీ} \te{కలుద్దాం}.} & \emph{maḷḷī kaluddām} & We'll meet again. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A few of these characters have not had their own lesson yet. They are here to be \textbf{recognised}, not decoded — the romanization beside each line is what you read from. The letters catch up in the chapters ahead.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the everyday goodbye — \emph{veḷḷi vastānu} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item the warm reply — \emph{veḷḷi raṇḍi} (\textquotedblleft{}go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — \emph{rēpu kaluddām}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{} — \emph{maḷḷī kaluddām}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — the atoms}]
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two verbs (\emph{veḷḷu} go, \emph{vaccu} come)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}again,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}let's meet\textquotedblright{} (\emph{rēpu}, \emph{maḷḷī}, \emph{kaluddām})
  \item the \textquotedblleft{}let's \_\_\_\textquotedblright{} ending (\emph{-ddām})
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Roots you now carry:}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{veḷḷi vastānu} — \textquotedblleft{}having gone, I come\textquotedblright{}; the Dravidian promise-of-return goodbye
  \item \emph{rēpu} \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} + \emph{kalu} \textquotedblleft{}meet\textquotedblright{} (native, where Tamil borrowed \emph{sandi})
  \item \emph{maḷḷī} $\leftarrow$ \emph{maral} \textquotedblleft{}to return\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does Telugu never say a plain \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving,\textquotedblright{} and what does its everyday goodbye promise instead? (It sounds too final; \emph{veḷḷi vastānu} promises \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
